A1-A2.headline: The Story of the Olympic Games

pages.text: The Olympic Games are huge sports events held around the world. They include Summer Games and Winter Games. Thousands of athletes from more than 200 teams take part in them. These teams represent different countries and territories.
pages.caption: An ice hockey game during the 1928 Winter Olympics at St. Moritz

imageProvenance.credit: Unknown authorUnknown author Unknown authorUnknown author

evidence.articleCaption: An ice hockey game during the 1928 Winter Olympics at St. Moritz

pages.text: The modern games were inspired by ancient Greek festivals held in Olympia. Baron Pierre de Coubertin started the International Olympic Committee in 1894. This group leads the Olympic movement and makes the rules for the games.
pages.caption: Pierre de Coubertin, co-founder of the International Olympic Committee and its second president

evidence.articleCaption: Pierre de Coubertin, co-founder of the International Olympic Committee and its second president

pages.text: The first modern games took place in Athens in 1896. Later, the games grew very large. Nearly every nation is now represented, and athletes compete for gold, silver, and bronze medals.

Over time, the games expanded to include winter sports like ice hockey and figure skating. A separate Winter Olympics was created. There are also youth games for younger athletes and other special events.
pages.caption: Jesse Owens on the podium after winning the long jump at the 1936 Summer Olympics, where he won four gold medals; in his 1980 obituary, The New York Times called him "perhaps the greatest and most famous athlete in track and field history".

imageProvenance.credit: Unknown authorUnknown author Unknown authorUnknown author

pages.text: Organizing such events brings many challenges, including boycotts, doping, match fixing, bribery, and terrorism. Still, the Olympics and their media exposure provide athletes with the chance to attain national and international fame every two years.

The modern Olympic Games are premier international multi-sport events divided into Summer and Winter editions. They feature thousands of athletes representing over 200 sovereign states and territories, often replacing world championships during their respective years.

pages.text: Inspired by ancient Greek religious and athletic festivals in Olympia, the modern movement was shaped by Baron Pierre de Coubertin. He founded the International Olympic Committee in 1894, which led to the first modern games in Athens in 1896 with support from Greek benefactors.
pages.caption: Pierre de Coubertin, co-founder of the International Olympic Committee and its second president

evidence.articleCaption: Pierre de Coubertin, co-founder of the International Olympic Committee and its second president

pages.text: The twentieth and twenty-first centuries brought major changes. The IOC shifted from pure amateurism to accepting professional athletes. World wars caused cancellations, and political tensions led to boycotts during the Cold War.

To accommodate snow and ice sports, the Winter Olympics were established as a separate event in 1924. After 1992, the Winter and Summer Games were staggered two years apart. The IOC also introduced the Youth Olympic Games and other inclusive sports festivals.

pages.text: Today, nearly every nation participates in the Olympics. While media exposure and commercial sponsorship provide global platforms for athletes and host cities, the movement continues to navigate modern challenges like doping, financial costs, and logistical shifts.

C1-C2.headline: History and Structure of the Olympics

pages.text: The modern Olympic Games constitute a preeminent international multi-sport institution comprising distinct Summer and Winter cycles. Engaging thousands of athletes across more than 200 national delegations, the Games operate under the governance of the International Olympic Committee.
pages.caption: An ice hockey game during the 1928 Winter Olympics at St. Moritz

imageProvenance.credit: Unknown authorUnknown author Unknown authorUnknown author

evidence.articleCaption: An ice hockey game during the 1928 Winter Olympics at St. Moritz

pages.text: Tracing its intellectual lineage to ancient Hellenic festivals in Olympia, the contemporary iteration was catalyzed by Pierre de Coubertin in 1894. Early financial foundations relied heavily on Greek trusts and benefactors to restore the Panathenaic Stadium for the inaugural 1896 Games.
pages.caption: Pierre de Coubertin, co-founder of the International Olympic Committee and its second president

evidence.articleCaption: Pierre de Coubertin, co-founder of the International Olympic Committee and its second president

pages.text: Throughout the twentieth century, the Olympic Movement underwent profound structural transformations. Economic pressures, the abandonment of strict amateurism, and commercialization reshaped participation. Geopolitical conflicts necessitated cancellations during world wars and prominent boycotts during the Cold War era.

Logistical demands prompted the bifurcation of the schedule in 1994, separating the Winter and Summer editions by a two-year interval within each Olympiad. Further diversification manifested through the establishment of the Youth Olympic Games and tailored programs for athletes with disabilities.

title: Tracing the Roots of Democratic Rule
attribution: Adapted from English Wikipedia contributors; see pinned revision and history. SAGA AI-assisted adaptation under CC BY-SA 4.0. Wikipedia does not endorse SAGA.

pages.text: Democracy is a system of government where people share power. In a modern democracy, citizens can change society and hold their leaders to the law. Long ago, ancient Greece tried early forms of democracy that changed politics forever.
pages.caption: The establishment of universal male suffrage in France in 1848 was an important milestone in the history of democracy.

evidence.articleCaption: The establishment of universal male suffrage in France in 1848 was an important milestone in the history of democracy.

pages.text: Long before cities existed, small groups of hunter-gatherers made choices together. These groups had about fifty to one hundred people. They often reached agreement without a chief. People call this early form of primitive democracy or tribalism.

Other ancient places also used assemblies. In ancient Mesopotamia, city-states had councils of elders and free men. These groups held final political power. They had to talk about big issues, like war, before making any choices.

Athens is famous as the birthplace of democracy. The word comes from Greek words for common people and force. Solon was an important lawmaker in Athens who helped create a system where citizens could attend a public assembly and vote.

In Athens, famous thinkers like Socrates, Plato, and Aristotle studied different types of rule. Aristotle wrote about systems run by one person, a few people, or many people. Their ideas helped shape political philosophy for a very long time.

B1-B2.headline: Tracing the Roots of Democratic Rule

pages.text: Democracy is a political system where members share power, allowing citizens to intervene in society and hold leaders accountable. While modern representative systems use social contracts to balance state power and individual rights, democracy is widely associated with ancient Greek experiments.
pages.caption: The establishment of universal male suffrage in France in 1848 was an important milestone in the history of democracy.

evidence.articleCaption: The establishment of universal male suffrage in France in 1848 was an important milestone in the history of democracy.

pages.text: Long before sedentary societies emerged, small bands of hunter-gatherers practiced proto-democracy. In groups of fifty to one hundred closely tied individuals, decisions were reached through consensus or majority rule, frequently without naming a specific chief.

Ancient civilizations also experimented with governing by assembly. In pre-Babylonian Mesopotamia, ultimate power rested with free male citizens. City-states relied on councils of elders and young men who possessed final political authority and had to approve major issues like war.

Athens is traditionally regarded as the birthplace of democracy, deriving its name from the Greek words for the common people and might. Lawmakers like Solon divided citizens into property classes and established the Ecclesia, an assembly where all citizens could vote on laws and elect officials.

The democratic environment of Athens fostered the growth of political philosophy. Philosophers like Socrates, Plato, and Aristotle analyzed various systems of rule. Aristotle famously categorized governments based on whether power rested with one person, a few, or the many.

Democracy constitutes a system of shared institutional power distinguishing itself through citizen intervention and sovereign accountability. Eighteenth-century revivalists resurrected ancient Greek ideals to construct post-monarchical templates, fundamentally transforming the international political landscape over subsequent centuries.
pages.caption: The establishment of universal male suffrage in France in 1848 was an important milestone in the history of democracy.

pages.text: Anthropological evidence indicates that primitive democracy or tribalism predates agrarian civilization. Small hunter-gatherer bands typically reached consensus or majority decisions within face-to-face community settings, frequently operating without designated chiefs.

Historical records from early Mesopotamia reveal loose power structures where ultimate authority resided with free male citizens. Major city-states utilized councils of elders and armed youth that maintained final political jurisdiction and required consultation on matters of war.

Athenian institutional evolution formalized popular sovereignty through figures like Solon, who established property classes and empowered the Ecclesia. This sovereign assembly acquired responsibilities for legislation, judicial appeals, and magistrate elections within a mixed timocratic framework.

The Athenian milieu catalyzed foundational political philosophy. Philosophers such as Plato and Aristotle scrutinized systemic rule types, with Aristotle systematically dividing governance into autocracy, oligarchy, and democracy based on the numerical distribution of ruling power.

title: How Advertising Grew Over Time
attribution: Adapted from English Wikipedia contributors; see pinned revision and history. SAGA AI-assisted adaptation under CC BY-SA 4.0. Wikipedia does not endorse SAGA.

pages.text: Advertising has a very long history. People used it in ancient times. Egyptians used papyrus to make sales messages. Walls and rocks were also painted with ads. Today, we can still see old rock art paintings in Asia, Africa, and South America.
pages.caption: Digital advertising technologies support the real-time bidding infrastructure used in digital display advertising

evidence.articleCaption: Digital advertising technologies support the real-time bidding infrastructure used in digital display advertising

pages.text: In ancient China, people used oral messages and signs to sell items. Merchants used bamboo flutes to sell candy. They also used paper posters and inked plates. One old plate from the Song dynasty used a rabbit logo for a needle shop.
pages.caption: Bronze plate for printing an advertisement for the Liu family needle shop at Jinan, Song dynasty China. It is considered the world's earliest identified printed advertising medium.

evidence.fileTitle: File:Bronze printing plate for an advertisement.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Bronze plate for printing an advertisement for the Liu family needle shop at Jinan, Song dynasty China. It is considered the world's earliest identified printed advertising medium.

pages.text: In the Middle Ages in Europe, many people could not read. Workers used pictures on signs instead of words. A boot meant a cobbler, and a horseshoe meant a blacksmith. Town criers also walked around to announce where fruit and vegetables were sold.

Modern advertising began with newspapers and magazines. The first weekly gazettes appeared in Europe in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries. Newspapers carried ads to help pay for printing costs. Early ads promoted books and medicines.

In the nineteenth century, advertising grew fast in the United States. Volney B. Palmer opened the first ad agency in Philadelphia. He bought newspaper space and resold it. Later agencies began to create complete ad campaigns with memorable slogans.
pages.caption: Advertising revenue as a percent of US GDP shows a rise in audio-visual and digital advertising at the expense of print media.

evidence.articleCaption: Advertising revenue as a percent of US GDP shows a rise in audio-visual and digital advertising at the expense of print media.

pages.text: In the twentieth century, new technologies changed advertising. Radio, television, and mobile devices brought ads to many people. Psychologists also helped advertisers understand how people think. Today, ads are a big part of the global economy.

The history of advertising dates back to ancient civilizations, where merchants used various methods to reach buyers. Egyptians utilized papyrus for sales messages, while wall paintings and rock art were common across Asia, Africa, and South America, with traditions dating back thousands of years.

pages.text: Ancient China recorded early forms of advertising through oral announcements, signboards, and printed papers. A copper printing plate from the Song dynasty, featuring a rabbit logo for a needle shop, is considered the world's earliest identified printed advertising medium.
pages.caption: Bronze plate for printing an advertisement for the Liu family needle shop at Jinan, Song dynasty China. It is considered the world's earliest identified printed advertising medium.

evidence.articleCaption: Bronze plate for printing an advertisement for the Liu family needle shop at Jinan, Song dynasty China. It is considered the world's earliest identified printed advertising medium.

pages.text: During the Middle Ages in Europe, widespread illiteracy led tradespeople to use symbols rather than words on their signs. A boot represented a cobbler, and a horseshoe stood for a blacksmith. Meanwhile, town criers walked through city streets to announce where goods were available.

Modern advertising began to develop with the introduction of newspapers and magazines in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries. These publications carried advertisements to offset printing and distribution costs, initially promoting books and medicines before expanding to a wider variety of products.

In the nineteenth century, the growth of industrialization in the United States created a massive supply of manufactured goods. To find consumers for these products, companies turned to mass marketing. Advertising agencies emerged, transitioning from simple space brokers to firms that planned complete advertising campaigns.

pages.text: As the twentieth century progressed, new media like radio and television transformed the industry. Psychologists applied behavioral theories to advertising, focusing on basic human emotions and suggestions. American agencies also expanded globally, establishing a worldwide presence to support large manufacturing companies.

Tracing its origins to antiquity, advertising has long served commercial and political functions. Early manifestations included Egyptian papyrus notices, urban displays in Pompeii, and rock art traditions across Asia, Africa, and South America that originated millennia ago.

pages.text: Early commercial communication in China combined oral promotion with calligraphic signboards and printed media. Notably, a copper printing plate from the Song dynasty featuring a distinct rabbit trademark represents the earliest known printed advertising medium.
pages.caption: Bronze plate for printing an advertisement for the Liu family needle shop at Jinan, Song dynasty China. It is considered the world's earliest identified printed advertising medium.

pages.text: Amid medieval European urbanization and widespread illiteracy, merchants relied on pictorial trade insignia instead of text. Concurrently, itinerant town criers announced merchant locations, a practice documented in contemporary poetry such as Les Crieries de Paris.

The advent of periodicals in sixteenth- and seventeenth-century Europe catalyzed modern advertising structures. Newspapers incorporated commercial notices to subsidize production expenses, progressively broadening their scope beyond early book promotions and quack remedies.

Nineteenth-century industrial expansion in the United States necessitated mass marketing strategies to absorb surplus manufactured output. Consequently, advertising agencies evolved from rudimentary space brokering into comprehensive firms executing complex promotional campaigns.

pages.text: Twentieth-century technological innovations, coupled with the integration of applied psychological theory, fundamentally transformed commercial persuasion. As domestic markets matured, prominent agencies pursued international expansion alongside industrial conglomerates, embedding advertising deeply within global capitalist economies.
